enter without pass from Mr. Jones, clerk

Chamberlain's men. About nine o'clock
General Gordon, United States senator from
Georgia, and General Johnson, state senator

members of the legislature, demanded ad-
mittance. The rotunda was filled with

sentinels who claimed to be elected member
of the legislature. Under this change of
orders, all the members were ad-
mitted slowly, as the corporal of the guard

to the hall of the senate or that of the house

with the Democrats. This leaves the house
without quorum.

the week and if more the week, we will

Judge of the district comprising Monroe and
Carbon counties, has been on the bench alone.
He was elected from Monroe County by a
unanimous vote, a rare compliment in a district
where partisan feeling is very strong. He is
about 50 years of age, and is of calm equable
and dispassionate temperament. He is evident
familiar with the law and practice, but listens
patiently to even the most prolix statement
of objections, often trivial and immaterial, and
avoids every opportunity to fortify such oblec-
tions by evidence and argument. If these pri-
soners do not have fair and impartial trial, it
will not be through any fault of Judge Dreher.

part of the work of preparing the case for the

arguments thus far in reply to the multifarious

PHILADELPHIA, August 14, &c.
Editors Register.


Whoever visits Niagara Falls think
they must immortalize themselves by
giving the public pen picture of them,
and in every instance the picture is
greatly inferior to the reality, and just
so with those who attempt to describe
the beauties of the Centennial. We
would advise all scribblers to stay at
home or desist from descriptive com-
munications while here. Every per-
son you meet upon the ground is armed
with a pencil and book noting every-
thing down so that they can the better
foist their wild jargon upon those who
cannot attend. We were standing be-
fore the petrified remains of mastodon
the other day, when upon glancing to
the right we found this description in
a lady's note book "The wonder of the
world, the remains of a giant Hyena
used by the Turks instead of horses, and
of the genus homo. He feasts upon the
heritage of tropical Russia and is as
docile as dog. This is the one that Dr.
Livingston rode on his travels in Africa."
This is the general style of note sketch-
ing, and from such notes who would ex-
pect much of communication.


WEST VIRGINIA


First called me to her friendly roof and
sure enough we found the "Latch string
out" and right proud did we feel as we
compared her achievements with those of
holder and wealthier states. Her miner-
als are of superior quality and her coal
takes the cap off of everything we have
yet seen here. The samples of our native
woods, although not so large as from
other sections, go far toward making our
display. The display of West Virginia
woods is good and we are inclined to
think G. H. Beal, of Brook and J. N.
Bell of Ohio have the finest samples of
wool, and after them comes John In-
gram of Poplar Springs.


All SIN


and his Chinese pig-tailed, acknowledged,
sandal-shanked creatures are as numer-
ous and disgusting as so many islander
dogs of oriental climes. The opium
loving Turk is here, with his far-inched
pipes and tobacco. France, with her
innumerable bottles of wine and brandy,
is here in vast numbers; while Italy
charms the ear with oriental strains and
the eye with ancient works by the old
masters. The Briton is here, with his
boosting, and the German with his power.


We have seen much, as, too much to
attempt to write letter, and we expect
against this time next week to be at
subject for Fairmont or Weston. We
have come far and gazed upon enough
to prostrate the strongest mind of all
time, but still we survive and flourish
upon Twelfth street, near Wood.

People live as long or longer that take spirituous liquor moderately; but must confess there is more hypocrisy about drinking spirituous liquors than ANYTHING else. A poor devil is brought before a court for selling or drinking liquor and often fined heavily and confined to Jail by men who drink themselves. There cannot be as great a sin in drinking liquor as they would have you believe, if we look back at the history of the human family. It tells you Adam had sons, and that Cain killed his brother Abel to end the first sin; but it don't say whether or not Cain had a jug of rum in the vineyard. There is no charge against him for this first sin of murder. Then it tells you as the human family increased in numbers it increased in degradation (mind no charge of rum being the cause) until God seriously meditated and decided to destroy that set of fellows with water, and that he set Noah to build, or experimenting the building of a boat called an ark. When it was finished he took in provisions, sea stores, stock and his own family to re-people the world after the deluge. (Some say General Grant has Noah in his family, when he appoints so largely from his own family.) It says the water came, they battled about for some time, finally landed on Mount Ararat, and that Noah got drunk and one of his sons that he saved from drowning laughed at him and that he, Noah, would curse him.

Now in this whole matter of deluge, there is not the strongest presumptive evidence, that the drinking of intoxicating liquors formed no part of the accumulated sins that caused God to deluge the world, for if it had, why did an all seeing and all knowing God, appoint a drunkard to build, or superintend the building of an ark, and allow the offspring of a drunkard to re-people the world. Next we run on for many hundred years, drinking wine and gives you this caution to not put new wine in old bottles; there was danger of bursting not glass, of course, but skin or leathern bottles, of course as the wine fermented there was danger of the stitching giving way. The world run on until the people again got in trouble, and they tell us God sent his Son to save the sinful world, and I believe it is not denied that His miracle was to turn water to wine. If water at a feast or dance would liven up the fun loving assembly, what was there in turning water to wine? Away with this hulaballoo about the sin of drinking intoxicating liquors. Use persuasion and example to restrain excessive and unnecessary drinking or eating, and drop the foolish idea of reform by laws. After great blowing of trumpets and any amount of gassy dragging, political temperance reformers nominated a candidate this centennial year for President, named Smith, and he received 10,051 votes out of a total of 2,515,150 votes, or in other words one out of every 2,500 votes cast. At that rate, these political temperance men will find Jordan a long road to travel.

I protest against our Legislature's waste of time in considering the schemes of fanatics. SAMUEL TOWNSEND.

Townsend, Dec. 10, 1876.

As she walked with Courtnay, Lady Diana had one beautiful trick, which I always admired, of holding his arm and turning to look at him with her head thrown back like a deer. Her heavy glorious hair had given her certain carriage of the head which was very noble. As she walked away, one day, leaning on his arm, I noticed this attitude especially. It seemed to me that she was adoring Courtnay far more than he did her.

The lessons went on unremittingly, and, one day, when Courtnay had left us for a journey to Milan, I ventured to speak of his extraordinary beauty, and to show her. Lady Diana was highly delighted, and proposed that we should both ask him to sit, and that she should sketch him in water-color, while I attempted him, in sort of Titianesque oils, in a sort of dress. Courtnay was very good-natured under this joint infliction, and posed for us patiently. He was indeed a subject worthy of work, and a perfect representation of Venetian nobility. I have never seen a more superb masculine beauty. To see the woman who loved him so tenderly, and with sort of attempted concealment of her passion—to see her gracious, noble, and aristocratic head thrown back as she looked at him with an artist's comprehension and woman's adoration, was the most worthy picture I have ever seen. I sat up nights to paint her from memory, and have the sketch by me still. We made two pictures of the same man totally unlike each other. Mine was the best picture and the most like him I still think; but, what would it do, it would look like Caesar Borgia. I got in Courtnay's eyes, but they had a hateful luster.

"You have made me a very handsome fellow, with very cunning, bad look," he said.

Lady Diana had given him the expression of an angel. Those black eyes shone in sort of liquid beatitude. I could not flor have never seen her.

power over the weather, that power would be

on the suns rays, by attraction, or by emana'

never equal in intensity or quality to that

That the moon does exert attraction on US is

but Though it can move water, it is most un-

stir the atmosphere at quicker rate than five
miles day. As for lunar emanations, not
sign of them has ever been discovered. The

phases of the moon is therefore based on no

ment of meteorological stations all over the

yations that there is no simultaneousness what
ever between the supposed cause and the sup.
posed effect The whole story is fancy and
superstition, which has been handed to US un-

THE RECONSTRUCTED STATES.

The thirteen reconstructed states cast ninety-five electoral votes, or more than one fourth of the whole number. All these states voted for Grant in 1868, except Georgia and Louisiana, which voted for Seymour, and Mississippi, Virginia, and Texas, which then not being fully restored to the Union, did not vote at all. For several years nine of those States were strongholds of the Republican party, but they have gradually become Democratic until at the present time the Republicans have a rather feeble hold upon only South Carolina, Florida and Louisiana.

In the pending Presidential campaign the reconstructed states are the key to the position; and unless the Republicans defeat the Democrats in three or four of the states now held by the latter, there is no hope of escape. Hence the look upon Mississippi, Arkansas, Louisiana, and Alabama with covetous eye; and if violent counsels prevail they will resort to the desperate expedient of the bayonet for recovering their lost ground in the South.

of voting by States, a rule which is
so distinctively consonant with the
autocratic and unanimic spirit of the
Democratic party.

lection of Hendricks would seem to
many of the party to be desirable as
a sort of compromise on the money

will not accept the second place on

hotly contested contest than any that

nation such additional strength will
render the result extremely doubtful.

The discussion Of the question Of


hanging or no hanging has called out


some very well written and able cdi-


torials in the Iowa press. We note


that the Dubuqc Times for, and the


Sioux City Journal against reviving


capital punishment, have argued up.


on the question at length, and quite
ably. This question has been dis.
cussed pro and con for many years
and perhaps nothing new can be adj.
vanced upon either side. We will,
therefore, only state our own convic-


tions upon il, with our reasons in


brief. It is our opinion that the old


statute Of this State was about the


best that could be devised. Under il
convictions for murder in the first
degree were very rare, and only for
cases where life had been taken with
the greatest deliberation, entirely free
from the heat OF sudden passion. In
such cases, especially where the act Ii
attended with atrocions and cruel
circumstances, in the present state and
condition Of society, the populace
have, and will seek the life Of the
murderer by Judge Lynch's process,
If the law does not provide for the
death penalty.


1t seems utterly impossible to avoid
instances of this kind sometimes, even
when the laws authorize capital pun
ishment, aud especially will this
lynching occur where the laws do not
permit the judgment of death. How
ever, we may theorize as to what are
proper laws, 1t Is truism that they
must be shaped, in doubtful cases, in
the light of theory, so in accordance
with public opinion, that they will
not be disregarded. Therefore we
say, without urging the force of the ar
gnment, that the death penalty serves
to prevent murder by the vicious
that we believe there will be a better
observance Of law, and really be less
hanging with law authorizing it in
extreme cases, than under law total
ly abolishing such punishment. We
are thoroughly Of the opinion, taking
society as it now Is, and as such, we
must legislatc for 1.-THE highest
standard of good order and good
government is best promoted by q
law authorizing capital punishment
in cases of cold blooded and premed-
itated murder. Whether it be abb
stractly right to take life, even under
the forms of law or not, is not ques-
ton we deem necessary to argue,
since there are so many good reasons
which may be advanced upon either
side. In the midst of such variety
of views upon this abstract question,
we choose to lay that aside, and de-
eide The matter as to whether we
shall have laws permitting capital

The discussion of the question of

hanging or no hanging has called out

some very well written and able editorials in the Iowa press. We note

that the Dubuque Times for, and the

Sioux City Journal against reviving

capital punishment, have argued upon the question at length, and quite

ably. This question has been discussed pro and con for many years

and perhaps nothing new can be advanced upon either side. We will,

therefore, only state our own convictions upon it, with our reasons in

brief. It is our opinion that the old

statute of this State was about the

best that could be devised. Under it

convictions for murder in the first

degree were very rare, and only for

cases where life had been taken with

the greatest deliberation, entirely free

from the heat of sudden passion. In

such cases, especially where the act is

attended with atrocious and cruel

circumstances, in the present state and

condition of society, the populace

have, and will seek the life of the

murderer by Judge Lynch's process,

if the law does not provide for the

death penalty.

instances of this kind sometimes, even

when the laws authorize capital punishment, and especially will this

lynching occur where the laws do not

permit the judgment of death. However, we may theorize as to what are

proper laws, it is a truism that they

must be shaped, in doubtful cases, in

the light of theory, so in accordance

with public opinion, that they will

not be disregarded. Therefore we

say, without urging the force of the argument, that the death penalty serves

to prevent murder by the vicious

that we believe there will be a better

observance of law, and really be less

hanging with law authorizing it in

extreme cases, than under law totally

abolishing such punishment. We

are thoroughly of the opinion, taking

society as it now is, and as such, we

must legislate for it. THE highest

standard of good order and good

government is best promoted by a

law authorizing capital punishment

in cases of cold blooded and premeditated murder. Whether it be abstractly right to take life, even under

the forms of law or not, is not a

question we deem necessary to argue,

since there are so many good reasons

which may be advanced upon either

side. In the midst of such variety

of views upon this abstract question,

we choose to lay that aside, and decide the matter as to whether we

shall have laws permitting capital

punishment or not, by the practical

issues involved, taking the condition

of society as it is.

The smoke of battle having cleared away we are enabled to see the objects and purposes and the losses and gains in our late municipal election in their true light. While the advantage gained last spring over that party regarded as opposed to the true interests of the city have not been maintained in the recent contest for city officers, yet the friends of the city achieved partial victory and are fortunate in having elected a majority of the city council. It is not our present purpose to go over the ground and speak ever in a general way of the mistakes made in conducting the late election on the side of the Citizens Association. Most of the errors are so attributable to the men who aided largely last year in making the fight against the Union League a complete success, resulting in a grand triumph for the good government of our city, were this year quietly told to step aside because they were Republicans. They could vote, and aid in this way, but to make themselves prominent would be, it was said, fatal to the cause in hand. In accordance with the detestable spirit thus manifested, an issue as uncalled for as it was unjust, and as ungenerous as it was vindictive was raised against Mr. J. T. Moak, street commissioner from the 1st ward, by those conducting the campaign on the side in opposition to The Citizens Association. The clamor raised against Mr. Moak, and through him against Republicans generally, found too much effect upon men who, while sincere in the stand they had taken with the Citizens Association, could not wholly divest themselves of party spirit and paid too much attention to the partisan cry of a few political mountebanks. Through the shibboleth raised against Republicans, Mr. Moak and his friends found themselves in the awkward position of feeling favorable to a cause where their countenance and support were scarcely desired. Mr. Moak was requested to stand aloof from a contest in which he certainly had as deep an interest as a majority of our citizens, solely, and for no other reason, than because he was Republican, and as the head of the movement against the League last spring, had fought out a campaign that not only reflected credit on his ability and judgment, but rebounded to the best and truest interests of the city. But he must be struck down and made a victim to foul party spirit and jealousy, no matter if in consequence, the cause which our citizens held most dear should suffer and be defeated. Even his an able and faithful member of the Common Council, and that his presence again in the board of street commissioners was almost indispensable to the success of the city government the coming year. Mr. Moak, however, approaching fully the thanklessness of the position, had determined months before, not to again come forward as a candidate for alderman, and under no consideration could he be made to. Under any circumstances would have been equivalent to an election. All the honors attached to the office of alderman, Mr. Moak reaped years ago, and his presence in the council of late years has been solely the act of his friends who, recognizing his ability and watchfulness saw him fit and proper man to be placed in position where he could be of benefit to the city. Had Mr. Moak put himself forward for reelection, or had he been derelict of his duty while in office, the shafts of malignity and vituperation hurled at him during the late campaign might have been excusable to a certain degree, but as his wishes regarding a re-election could not have been misunderstood, nor could anything be said against his official acts, the abuse heaped upon Mr. Moak can only be explained on the ground of pure political cussedness coupled with a disposition too often prevalent in communities of striking man down because he is doing too much good. Mr. Moak retires this spring from the office of Street Commissioner with great credit to himself, and carries with him to his retirement the thanks of the vast majority of our citizens for his arduous and distinguished services in behalf of the city's interests. The city of Watertown cannot well afford to lose the services of such public servants as Mr. Moak has proved to be.

Office of Lancaster & Lucke, No. 111 Main street.

The valuable property known as the lands and tenements of Messrs. M. & J. L. Lancaster, thirty-four acres in fee simple and one third of six acres, the company holds undivided interests and easements and an interest in the machinery and implements used herewith, and also the CLOVER HILL RAILROAD, which is twenty-one miles in length, running from Clover Hill Mines to Osbornes, on James River, with all its rights and privileges and coal reservoir. All of the above property will be sold whole, and lists of the same in detail have been printed and will be furnished to all.

Special Commissioner.

the departing rays of the setting sun illuminated the western sky the last remains of the lion hearted and Christian gentleman, Gen. Braxton Bragg, were carried to their last resting place in Magnolia Cemetery, near Mobile. No living chieftain so strong in the memory of victory, ever received all the hands of his faithful followers, more spontaneous outbursts of loyal and enthusiastic devotion than did this dead hero, from the city destined to be his burial place, loving hearts and tender hands struggled to do him honor.

Editors Of the Times:

Many Of your readers are doubtless ignorant of the existence Of the town Of Birmingham. This would be excusable ignorance inasmuch as Birmingham has only secured place on the map Of Alabama within the last few years, and has little, as yet, TO make it known. THE FAMOUS RED MOUNTAIN.


About one mile to the east Of the town is the famous Red Mountain, which is from forty to fifty miles in length and noted as being the largest ore mountain in this country, and perhaps IN the world. On top Of this mountain and extending its entire length is the ore varying in thickness from fifteen to thirty feet. The ore is classed as fossiliferous red hematite, and has yielded under analysis from 40 to 90 per cent Of metallic iron. One cannot form even an approximate idea Of the extent OF the ore without an examination, and what attracts the practical iron man is the facility with which it can be mined. ORE FOR TWENTY CENTS A TON

Washington Is left desolate


THE CAPITAL WITHOUT CONGRESS


resembles Goldsmiths deserted village. that the town is left, but the principal inhabitants are gone. By the haste with which everybody rushed to the railroad the morning after the adjournment of Congress—one would fancy that the cars, like Cinderella's coach, would be changed into pumpkins at the stroke of twelve. The town was evacuated in a day. On the next placard was sent back by the hotel keepers at PHILADELPHIA declaring that there was not so much as a garret to be had in that city, and imploring ladies and gentlemen to remain quietly in Washington for twenty-four hours. Young ladies were seen at the depot with long faces, leaving the delights of Washington for the dull repose of the COUNTRY, their lovers with longer faces trying to solve the problem expressed by their still longer bills—and members of Congress with long faces too, for not one in twenty has made the impression he expected, and he departs moralizing on the decline in the taste for eloquence and on the want of a golden opportunity for the display of indignant virtue.


When Congress and its ten thousand casual visitors are gone, and only the official and indigenous inhabitants remain, nothing can look more desolate. He who would be reminded of departed friends should walk down the avenue viewing those charmed spots of gay resort whose gayety has departed, the numerous frequented places that shall know the oft-time visitor no more in December. The person for whom the desolation is the unkindest cut of all is the hack-driver. His occupation is gone indeed. Gone is the dollar made every successive half-hour, gone are the short but profitable trips to the theatre, gone the four or five families all taken the same evening to parties and each paying the item of carriage from nine till twelve, and gone the absorbed politician who would rather give the five dollar bill than wait for the change. The chop-chair coach drives to his stand in the morning and creeps home to dinner; night comes on and his horses begin to believe in the millennium, while the cobwebs are woven over his whip-socket.


The President and family return to happiness and Long Branch to spend the close of that long summer, the greater part of which they have been prevented from enjoying by the long drawn-out session. Newspaper Row is deserted, attaches grow fat and dispatches grow lean, as the reporters slip away to Cape May or the White Sulphur. We who are left have the prospect of enjoying the most delightful portion of the year, as far as weather is concerned, from now until December as a recompense for our solitude, and in the never-failing delights of Washington autumn we are sure to be comforted and consoled for the loss of the crowd.


THE CLOSING HOURS OF CONGRESS


were not without their usual excitements, and even what might be considered as a nice little note was precipitated on Monday night in the House. On that evening the House was more than usually well filled, nearly all were looking for speedy adjournment and were, therefore, bound to see as much of Congress as possible, before the curtain fell. We found a vacant seat in the gallery about ten o'clock, while Mr. Kasson of Iowa was in the midst of his eloquent speech on the political situation. Every ear was strained to catch the speaker's words, both in the gallery and on the floor, as his subject was one in which all were deeply interested. Mr. Kasson is a polished speaker, the best of Anglo-Saxon, and never allows his feelings get the better of his judgment. Every one of his numerous and able speeches during the session have been especially remarkable for their candor and close application to the subject in hand. On this occasion he was replying to the attempt made by Sam Randall during the day to bolster up his own record as a leader of the majority in the House, by an eulogy of the Democratic party, and an excoriation of the Republican party. Mr. Kasson went through with a scathing rehearsal of the records of both Tilden and Hendricks based upon historical fact, which aroused the Democratic side of the House to a high pitch of frenzy. Hester Clymer, Randall and Sanders sought repeatedly to interrupt him, but made matters worse for their candidates at every attempt. When Kasson had finished, little Sammy Cox endeavored to get the floor, and finally succeeded. He started out with the assertion that Mr. Kasson was the apologist of Belknapp and the post-traders. Mr. Kasson called him to order for stating an untruth regarding members of the House. Cox then, in the most melodramatic style, rushed over to the Republican side up the aisle where Kasson sat, shook his fist in the latter's face, and called him a detestable liar, winding up by striking his eyeglasses with his finger and telling at the top of his voice that he had a letter from Gov. Tilden. Many of the more prominent Republicans were seated around Kasson, and had been listening to his speech. General Garfield sat at his left hand, Colonel Joyce directly at his right, and Henderson of Illinois, the next seat beyond, while Blair, Hunter, and Stevenson were in the next row front. The latter gentleman, as Cox came up to Kasson and uttered the objectionable word, threw himself between the two, fearing personal contest, while Mr. Blair promptly called Cox to order and asked that his words be taken down. This was done and Cox was given chance to apologize, which he accepted very soon after. Such a scene served to throw all ideas of business from the minds of the House and as consequence an adjournment was not reached until six o'clock in the morning. One of the surprises of the night was a speech from Mr. Hewitt, of New York, which, although such speech as many might be expected to make, was nevertheless an eloquent one and proclaimed Hewitt to be an orator of no ordinary ability. His looks are against all claims he may make to statesmanship, as his face, figure and actions resemble those of a proprietor of a first-class bar, but he has got the true fire of oratory within, and should be given the credit for one of the best impromptu speeches made this session.


THE WORK OF THE SESSION


has been very light in comparison to the number of days it has been convened. Three hundred laws have been passed, about evenly divided between public and private acts. Four thousand and ninety bills have been introduced in the House and one thousand and forty-six in the Senate. This is a larger number, we understand, than was ever introduced in Congress before at any one session. There are more private claims before this Congress than ever before, most of which come from the South. Every day of the next session will be required to get through with the work left over.


As to the work accomplished and concerning the principal workers in Congress—we must defer comment until next week.


PERSONAL AND POLITICAL


A dispatch has just been received here this evening announcing the death of Speaker Kerr. He has suffered the most intense agony throughout his illness, owing to the nature of his disease, irritation of the bowels, and death followed from sheer starvation and weakness. The remains are to be taken to the late residence of the deceased, New Albany, Indiana, on Monday, accompanied by the acting Speaker, Mr. Sayler. The death of the Speaker of the House necessitates an election at the opening of the next session, and Milton Sayler will most probably be elected, having shown an admirable fitness as presiding officer and being a favorite with the majority of the House.


Henry Wattersen, the editor of the Long Island Courier-Journal, was sworn in as member of the House the day before adjournment, to fill the vacancy made by the death of Representative Parsons, of Kentucky. He will be a man of merit next session, and has some claims to prominence both as an editor and presiding officer, and looks to be about thirty-five years of age, with an intellectual face, which is somewhat marred by a defect in the right eye, and well-defined features. The officer in charge at Fort Whipple is Lieut.
R. P. Strang. He is assisted by nine commis-
sioned officers, costing the Government nearly
$5000 per month. The most that these officers
do is to learn to read the barometer and swing
flags. They are busy only about an hour each
day, the rest of their time being mainly em-
ployed in loitering about the Washington bar
rooms. Lieut. Strang has lately had a fine house
built for him on the fort reservation, which cost
over $4,000, the same being paid for out of
funds appropriated by Congress for the Weather
Bureau. Strang was building the house all
last summer, quartering his mechanics in
the hospital, where they lived well, while
over at the barracks the "meteorological stu-
dents" were starving on rotten meat, bitter
bean coffee, and chunks of bread—a diet the
like of which old soldiers who have served at
decent military posts say they never saw before
they came to Fort Whipple. The poor devils
kept there have company fund they pay for
good food, but what they sit down to is such
that any decently brought up man on seeing it
would turn away and walk off with his tail
between his legs. Some of the men would like to
know whether it takes all the COMPANY fund to
pay for the red herrings that the starving fellows
are once in while recalled with as a luxury.

Whipple. On the one hand, big, salaried, nam-
pered army officers doing nothing, and on the
other, enlisted men, intelligent and well read,
many of them starved, abused, and thrown into
the dirty guard house like criminals, upon the
slightest provocation. The officers, so soon
as they learn to read the barometer, are sent out
inspecting tours, travelling from Maine to Texas,
the various signal stations, for the purpose of
seeing whether the sergeants have kept their
barometers clean. The sergeants in charge of
the stations stand in almost mortal dread of
these inspecting officers. They are obliged to
appear before them in a rag-tag and bobtail uni-
form and sometimes, when they have not got
the uniform to put on, they are punished by be-
ing sent way back to Fort Whipple, often at an
expense of $800 or more to the United States.
Vice are enormous. There is not a day that
Weather Bureau men do not arrive or depart
from the national capital, bound sometimes so
far away as Arizona, because somebody out
there has the rheumatism of limbs, and the

cost. Congress appropriated $300,000 for this

people really pay six times that amount, for the
purpose of being assisted in guessing whether it
is going to rain to-morrow. Bills dis-

whether it lives or dies; but if Gen. Myer is to
be allowed to continue the concern under the
belief that the management of the weather can-

house there sometimes because they have been
unable to prevent prisoners' escape when they
have been on duty. Others get two or three
months for offences that could be in no way
punishable in civil life. They are treated
worse than criminals, when hardly one of them
is not at least the equal of any of his superiors
in honesty and morality. They are obliged to

pay and can get drunk on better liquor.

A. I do not know when he left for Texas.

year, Col. Gibbs, the Lieutenant Governor
and Beverley Matthews at Matthews' office?
A. I saw Col. Gibbs and A. X. Davis at
Matthews' office, on Sunday, May 23, 1875.
Q. Did you see Col. Matthews?
A. I am not positive.
Q. Where did you see him?
A. I think I saw him in his office.
Q. Where were the other two?
A. Gibbs and Davis came out of Matthews'
office, on the sidewalk in front of Matthews'
office. Gibbs came across the street and
Davis called him back. They went into the
office and staid there, and never saw them
any more.

23, 1875?
A. Yes, sir.

May?

was some disturbance in our Index office.

and referred to the files had made on the
previous day.

were in the office after the Lieutenant
Governor had called Gibbs back?
A. No, sir.

sure, on the streets, sometime after that
day.

A. No, sir; by himself.

more that day—that is, all together?
A. No, sir.

Shoddy Mill, on st. John street, near
Germantown avenue, in the Quaker
City. 1t was four story building, and
unprotected by fire escapes. 1t was
stored with combustible rags and paper,
and fortunately when the fire broke out
only ten employees were in the building.
Of these Ellen Hever proved herself the
true heroine in her efforts to save the
lives of some poor girls employed in the
fourth story. Ellen Hever and four
others worked on the first floor. About
eight o'clock the fire broke out in the
second story, and the flames spread with
great rapidity. Mrs. Hever's compan-
ions fed Immediately, but the brave
young woman wished to save the lives
of the six women employed on the fourth
floor, and rushed up to give an alarm.
The flames confronted them on the sec
ond floor; but four of the women, with
remarkable presence of mind, dashed
through and jumped from window to
the roof of an adjoining shed and es-
capped. But another moment was fatal.
Poor Ellen and her two companions were
not so lucky. The flames completely
enveloped the track of their companions,
and the heat at once became so intense
that the unfortunate women had to re-
treat to the upper story. The scene
which ensued battles description. 1t
was truly heartrending. The crowd in
the street gazed upon the distracted
women rushing to and fro, the flames
about to encircle them at any moment,
and was powerless to save them. Their
cries were distracting. The flames drove
them to the fourth floor, and the excited
crowd shouted "Jumpl Jump!" 1t

jump. Bales of rags and shoddy were
placed on the sidewalk, and Ann Pat
terson made the fatal leap. The other
two women secureda rope which reached
to the third story, and the heroine, Ellen
Hever, and Maria Hoover, one after the
other, dropped from the third story upon
the pavement. Poor Ellen died few
minutes after, Ann Patterson an hour
later, and Maria Hoover, like the two
other unfortunates, was SO terribly man.
gled that her life was despaired of. She
is probably dead ere this. Ellen Hever
proved herself a true heroine. She
might easily have escaped, but could
not see others in peril. She was mar
ried woman, thirty-three years of age,
and had seven children to support. The
Philadelphians will amply provide for
them.

should teach Philadelphia lesson. She
has many hundreds of factories without

the lives of working people in them.
